rows.sentence: This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors.
For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency.
The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion.
Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability.
These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.
A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame.
These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.
Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines.

The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.

Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems.
On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.
On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards.
Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.
Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.
The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted.
On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications.
Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.
Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.
The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.

The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.
Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.
Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.
Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.
Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications.
The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses.
These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion.
This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

BASS (PSI-26): closest configuration SIBAL fabric (1–2 cm), concurrent and opposed flow; flow match 0.90 (flow concurrent; opposed, up to 40 cm/s, named in the PSI record, not a test value); research purpose match 1.00 (role prevention; suppression).

PSI has no partial-gravity (lunar or Martian) combustion data; every result here is a microgravity test. The challenge statement suggests that results at the two ends of the gravity scale could bound intermediate levels. This page does not treat them as bounds: in NASA drop-tower tests of three materials (Olson and Ferkul 2012, Table I), the oxygen limits at lunar gravity were lower than at both 0 g and 1 g, and at Martian gravity lower for two of the three. Those drops lasted 5.18 s and used extinction criteria that differ from the 1 g test. NASA names partial-gravity material flammability a major gap (OCHMO-TB-008). The challenge statement names the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment as expected future sources, and ACME's E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22) as an experiment in which an electric field mimicked partial gravity.
